articles.title: Firewall Zone Persistence: Why firewalld Runtime Changes Vanish and How to Pin Them
articles.excerpt: You run firewall-cmd --zone=public --change-interface=wlp2s0, firewalld answers success, and --get-active-zones shows the change. After the next reboot, a firewall-cmd --reload, or a Wi-Fi reconnect,…
articles.body: You run firewall-cmd --zone=public --change-interface=wlp2s0 , firewalld answers success , and --get-active-zones shows the change. After the next reboot, a firewall-cmd --reload , or a Wi-Fi reconnect, the interface is back in whatever zone it was in before. firewalld doesn't log anything about it. This isn't a bug. firewalld keeps two separate configurations, and on a NetworkManager system a third component also gets a say in which zone an interface belongs to. If you don't know about all three, any change you make by hand will eventually be undone. What I Expected My mental model was the iptables one: you run a command, the rule exists, and if you want it to survive a reboot you save it. I knew firewalld had a --permanent flag, so I assumed the fix was to tack it on and move on.
articles.author: Guatu

articles.title: I compared TinyPNG alternatives on privacy, not just file size
articles.excerpt: Everyone's used TinyPNG. It's the default "make this image smaller" tool, and its compression is genuinely good. But every roundup I read compares these tools on file size alone, and in 2026 that's th…
articles.body: Everyone's used TinyPNG. It's the default "make this image smaller" tool, and its compression is genuinely good. But every roundup I read compares these tools on file size alone, and in 2026 that's the least interesting difference between them. Here's the direct answer: the tools differ less on file size than on where your images get processed and what you pay. TinyPNG uploads your files to its servers and charges a subscription (Web Pro is $3.25/month billed annually — $39/year, verified on their pricing page today). Browser-local tools like Squoosh and SnapShrink process everything on your device. I build SnapShrink , a batch image compressor that runs 100% in the browser, and I'll tell you exactly where TinyPNG still wins.

articles.body: I'm a university student in Hong Kong. I spent two hours writing cold emails last week — between classes and assignments — trying to land some freelance clients. Every single one started with "Hi [FirstName], I hope you're doing well." I sent 40. I got zero replies. The problem wasn't the offer. It was that every email was obviously templated. You could smell it from the first line. And the people I was emailing — marketing directors, founders — get 50 of those a day. So I built a script to fix it. Here's how it works, and the code behind it. The Problem With Mail Merge Standard mail merge replaces [FirstName] with the actual name. That's not personalization. That's a template with a name plugged in.

articles.excerpt: How UI/UX Designers Can Build Scalable Income With Design Products If you're a UI/UX designer, there's a good chance your income is still closely tied to one thing: How many projects can you complete?…
articles.body: How UI/UX Designers Can Build Scalable Income With Design Products If you're a UI/UX designer, there's a good chance your income is still closely tied to one thing: How many projects can you complete? You finish a landing page. You get paid. You design a dashboard. You get paid. You redesign an app. You get paid. Then the project ends, and you start looking for the next client. There is nothing wrong with freelancing. Client work is one of the best ways to build experience, understand real business problems, develop a portfolio, and generate income. The problem appears when 100% of your income depends on continuously selling your time. A different approach is to turn some of the work you already know how to do into reusable design products.
